summary: Russia agrees to new Ukraine talks, an attack hits a Saudi airport, the UN says 1.5C will be breached, Brazil's runoff turns legal, Gantz quits Israel's race, and students protest AI.

topics.heading: Russia agrees in principle to new three-way talks with Ukraine and the US
topics.summary: After about three hours with US envoy Steve Witkoff, the Kremlin said it is ready in principle to resume talks with Ukraine and the US, the first since February. Russia also freed a jailed American, Stephen Hubbard.

lead.title: Trump envoy Witkoff meets Putin in St. Petersburg as Russia agrees to resume Ukraine talks

alsoReported.title: What happened during Witkoff and Kushner's latest meeting with Putin
Russia says Ukraine must make "necessary decisions" to end war as Witkoff meets Putin

article: On Wednesday, US envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg for about three hours, with Jared Kushner joining by video[^1]. Afterwards, Kremlin adviser Yuri Ushakov said Russia agreed "in principle" to restart three-way talks with the US and Ukraine after November 10, focused on a security system for both countries once the fighting ends[^1]. The Kremlin says the talks may be held in Abu Dhabi[^2].

The meeting opened with a gesture: Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired American teacher held for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine, after Trump asked Putin to free him[^1][^2]. Witkoff told Putin, "You are a humanitarian also, sir," which drew criticism in Washington, including from Republican Senator Thom Tillis[^2][^3].

Background: the last talks of this kind, in Abu Dhabi and Geneva early this year, produced little beyond prisoner exchanges[^1]. The two sides remain far apart. Ushakov said the ideas Witkoff brought from Ukraine's side "contained little of real value", though he later called them a step in the right direction[^1]. Kremlin officials, quoted by Russian state media, said a deal is possible only if Kyiv makes "necessary decisions"[^3].

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy backed restarting talks quickly, adding, "We'll see what happens this time"[^1]. He told Fox News he would reject any deal written by the US, Russia and China without Ukraine, and that Ukraine's parliament would have to approve any settlement[^3]. The war went on overnight: Kyiv's city authorities said Russian strikes killed three people there, and Russia said it shot down 373 Ukrainian drones[^1].

What could happen next: Norway's prime minister expects talks in mid-November[^1], and a possible Trump-Putin-Xi meeting at next month's APEC summit in China is still unconfirmed[^2]. My read: agreeing to talk is a real step, but the hard questions of territory and guarantees are still untouched.
topics.differences: Accounts of the timing differ: the AP quotes Ushakov as saying talks could resume after November 10, CBS reports "early November", and Norway's prime minister expects mid-November[^1][^3]. Russia frames the talks as Kyiv making "necessary decisions"; Zelenskyy says nothing can be decided about Ukraine without Ukraine[^3].

topics.heading: Deadly strike on Saudi Arabia's Dammam airport as the US orders staff to leave
topics.summary: An attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam killed one or two people, and the US told non-emergency embassy staff to leave Saudi Arabia. Iran's Revolutionary Guards say they hit seven ships in the Gulf.

lead.title: Middle East war: Saudi airport attack kills one as US orders embassy departures

alsoReported.title: Iran's IRGC Navy says seven vessels hit, warns US of wider response
Iran claims seven vessels hit in new wave of Hormuz attacks

article: On Wednesday evening, an attack hit King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, in Saudi Arabia's oil-rich east. Reports differ on the toll: Saudi Arabia's aviation authority was first reported as saying one person died and eight were hurt, while later updates said two died, a Saudi citizen and an Indian resident[^4][^7]. The authority says flights have returned to normal[^4]. No one has claimed the attack; it follows weeks of Houthi strikes on Saudi airports, though the Houthis have denied targeting deep inside the kingdom[^4][^7]. Separately, debris from an intercepted drone killed two foreign workers at the Shaybah oilfield, the Saudi energy ministry said[^4].

The US State Department ordered non-emergency government staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, citing threats from Yemen's Houthis[^7]. A diplomatic source told AFP the order was wider and included families in the UAE, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain[^4]; the State Department spokesman said it covers Saudi Arabia only[^7].

At sea, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said on Thursday that it hit four ships carrying out what it called illegal oil transfers in the northern Gulf, and that three more struck mines west of the Strait of Hormuz[^5]. Iran gave no ship names or evidence[^6]. The UK's maritime security agency, UKMTO, separately reported a tanker struck by a projectile off Oman, with its crew safe[^6]. The UN shipping agency now counts 119 security incidents and 24 seafarer deaths since the war began[^6]. The IRGC warned that the US could face a wider response against its regional bases[^5].

Diplomacy continues alongside: France's President Emmanuel Macron made a surprise visit to Riyadh, Egypt's parliament postponed its debate on helping defend Saudi Arabia, and Iran's foreign minister said Tehran is open to diplomacy if the US shows good faith[^4]. My read: civilian airports and the Gulf's oil routes are becoming the front line, which makes a mistake or a wider war more likely.
topics.differences: The death toll at Dammam is given as one in some reports and two in later updates[^4][^7]. On the US order, an AFP source describes a wide departure covering several Gulf states, while the State Department says it applies only to Saudi Arabia[^4][^7]. Iran's claim of seven ships hit is its own and has not been independently confirmed; the US military has previously disputed Iran's claims about mines[^6].

topics.heading: UN report says warming will pass 1.5C, but could be pulled back by 2100
topics.summary: For the first time, the UN Environment Programme says the world can no longer avoid passing 1.5C of warming. Its best case peaks at 1.7 to 1.8C and returns to 1.5C by 2100, but that needs deep cuts starting now.

lead.title: UN sets steep emission cuts to reverse 1.5C overshoot by end of century

alsoReported.title: Global warming will breach 1.5°C, UN report finds
UN report calls out US emissions, says world can no longer avoid overshooting key climate target

article: On Wednesday the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) published its yearly Emissions Gap Report, which compares what countries promise with what the science says is needed[^8]. Its main finding: decades of slow action mean warming will exceed 1.5C above pre-industrial levels, the limit the 2015 Paris Agreement aimed for[^8][^9]. UNEP's head, Inger Andersen, said the chance of holding warming below 1.5C "is now gone"[^10].

The report still sees a way back. In its lowest-overshoot path, warming peaks at about 1.7 to 1.8C around mid-century and falls back to 1.5C by 2100[^8][^9]. "Overshoot" means going over a limit for a while before coming back down. That path needs emissions cut 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, compared with 2025[^8]. It would also mean pulling about 320 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide out of the air this century, through forests and machines, which UNEP calls uncertain[^9].

Where things stand: global emissions were about 58.4 billion tonnes in 2025, roughly flat on 2024[^9][^10]. With current policies, warming could reach 2.8C this century; if every national plan is carried out, about 2.6C[^8]. The outlook is worse than last year's, partly because the US left the Paris Agreement[^8]. The report says the US was the only major economy whose emissions rose sharply in 2025; the US government said it does not agree with the analysis[^10].

There is also some good news in the report. Solar power has grown about seven times faster than forecasts made a decade ago, and coal and oil supply grew more slowly than projected[^8][^9]. UN Secretary-General António Guterres said "overshoot is not surrender" and called the emissions gap "a leadership gap"[^8][^10].

What comes next: countries meet at the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Türkiye, next month, where a new global review of progress begins[^8]. My read: every extra tenth of a degree matters, so the question is now how small and short the overshoot can be.

topics.heading: Brazil's close runoff turns into a fight over Meta and bids to disqualify rivals
topics.summary: Before Sunday's presidential runoff, Flávio Bolsonaro asked the electoral court to bar President Lula, and Lula's campaign said it would seek the same against Bolsonaro, accusing Meta of tilting its platforms.

lead.title: Lula, Bolsonaro seek to disqualify each other ahead of Brazil runoff

alsoReported.title: Meta tells Brazil's electoral court it gives equal treatment to Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro

article: Brazil votes on Sunday, October 25, in a presidential runoff between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, on the left, and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, on the right, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro[^11]. In the first round on October 4, Bolsonaro won 47% to Lula's 45%, and polls show a very close race[^11][^12].

In the final week, each side is trying to knock the other out in court. On Tuesday, Bolsonaro's lawyers asked the Superior Electoral Court to annul Lula's candidacy, accusing him of "abuse of power" through mass WhatsApp messages promoting government programmes[^11]. Lula's campaign said it would ask for Bolsonaro's disqualification over what it calls "algorithmic manipulation" by Meta, the company that owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp[^11].

The Meta dispute began on October 15, when Lula's campaign accused the company of using biased algorithms and AI tools to limit his content[^12]. On Monday the court gave Meta 24 hours to prove it treats both campaigns equally, with a daily fine of about $200,000 if not[^11]. Meta says it has complied, denies any political bias, and blames recent problems with Lula's ads on technical errors; it added human review of any automatic blocks on campaign ad accounts within two hours[^12].

Why it matters: Brazil is Latin America's largest country and economy, and this case tests how much power courts have over the platforms where most campaigning now happens. What could happen next: the court must decide on both disqualification requests, and the result on Sunday may be very close. My read: legal challenges are common in Brazilian elections, and few succeed this late, but they can shape whether the losing side accepts the result.
topics.differences: Lula's campaign says Meta's algorithms suppressed his content to help Bolsonaro; Meta denies bias and says the issues were technical[^11][^12]. Bolsonaro's side says Lula abused government messaging; Lula's side says Bolsonaro benefited from platform manipulation. Neither claim has been ruled on yet[^11].

topics.heading: Benny Gantz quits Israel's election race eight days before the vote
topics.summary: The former defence minister pulled his Blue and White party out of the October 27 election after polls kept showing it below the threshold to enter parliament. The move could help the bloc trying to replace Netanyahu.

lead.title: Benny Gantz quits Israel's election race eight days before vote

alsoReported.title: Gantz pulls out of election race, eight days ahead of vote
Israel Election 2026: Benny Gantz pulls out of race days before vote

article: On Monday, Benny Gantz, a former army chief and defence minister who leads the Blue and White party, said he will not run in Israel's October 27 election[^13][^14]. For months, polls showed his party below the 3.25% of the vote a party needs to win seats in the Knesset, Israel's parliament[^13]. Votes for a party below that line are wasted.

The timing was linked to soldiers' voting, which began the next day; a source close to Gantz said he did not want soldiers' votes to be lost[^13]. Gantz took responsibility, saying he had not convinced enough of the public, and said he will keep pushing for a "broad Zionist government" across political camps[^15]. On October 21, Blue and White's ballot slips were to be removed from polling stations after all its candidates quit[^14].

Background: Gantz has joined governments led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the past, and this week he said he did so despite Netanyahu, not because of him[^13]. Former allies, such as ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot, who now leads the Yashar party, thanked him for a "correct and responsible" decision[^13][^15]. Opposition leaders had urged him to step aside so that votes would not be wasted[^15].

Why it matters: this election is widely seen as a vote on Netanyahu, the Gaza war and the stalled ceasefire. What could happen next: it is unclear where Gantz's remaining voters will go; Eisenkot and Yoaz Hendel are both courting them[^15]. My read: one fewer small party helps the opposition, but Israeli elections are usually decided by the coalition talks that follow.

topics.heading: Students at more than 50 US campuses walk out to demand a freeze on AI
topics.summary: On Tuesday, students and some professors at colleges across the US walked out of classes to call for a pause on AI development until the public has a say, citing jobs, learning and safety.

lead.title: Students at SUNY Purchase join nationwide AI freeze walkout

alsoReported.title: 'It's a black box': Local students, professors plan walkout to demand freeze on AI development
Howard students plan walkout as part of 50-campus push demanding a freeze on AI development

article: On Tuesday, students at colleges across the United States walked out of class in a "National Walkout to Freeze AI"[^17][^18]. The organiser, a new national group called Irreplaceable, said more than 50 campuses were taking part, including Howard University in Washington[^17]. In Boston, students from schools such as MIT, Harvard and Northeastern rallied at the Massachusetts State House, and dozens of students joined at SUNY Purchase in New York[^16][^18].

Their main demand is a freeze on building more powerful AI "until the public has a say in how it is built and deployed"[^17]. They also want a share of AI's economic benefits and protections against catastrophic risks[^17]. Organisers say they modelled the campaign on the 1982 movement to freeze nuclear weapons, and groups such as the Sunrise Movement and National Nurses United support it[^17].

Students gave personal reasons. A computer science senior at SUNY Purchase said he worries AI will take entry-level coding jobs, and others raised concerns about learning: one student said, "People can't write basic essays"[^18]. A Boston organiser said students were told a degree meant "job security" and now are unsure[^16]. The Boston organisers said one trigger was a researcher who left Anthropic and OpenAI and warned publicly that AI companies were gambling with lives[^16].

Context and limits: the reports we read did not include responses from AI companies, and none explained how a freeze would work in practice or be enforced across countries[^16]. Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey has proposed safety testing and reporting rules for the most powerful AI models[^16]. My read: the walkout shows that worries about AI are spreading from experts to students, and that AI rules could become a voting issue for young people.

question.text: Iran says it hit seven ships, Meta says it treats both Brazilian candidates equally, and the Kremlin says talks are possible. When the main source for a claim is the side with the most at stake, what would you need to see before you believed it?

read.title: UN sets steep emission cuts to reverse 1.5C overshoot by end of century
read.summary: A clear walk-through of the new UN report: what "overshoot" means, the cuts needed by 2030, 2035 and 2040, and why relying on pulling carbon out of the air later is risky.
